module: Sharps (from BBP) · Public service: Law enforcement · New hire · Host and expert interview

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: One person, holding a used needle with the sharps container just down the hall, told themselves... "just this once." We'll be exploring the consequences of that decision today.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [warmly] I'm Dana.

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: I'm Ray. Glad you're with us.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [curious] Ray, you worked patrol for years before you moved into training new officers. When someone brand new shows up, what's the first thing you notice?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: How BADLY they want to get it right. And I can usually tell early on which little habits are going to stick with them.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [thinking out loud] Which is today's subject, really: the habits people build around needles and other sharp objects at work.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [curious] More people now inject their own medicine at work, for things like diabetes and allergies. Does that really reach a police station?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: It does. Accidental needle sticks are especially common in healthcare, but the risk is real and growing at other jobs too. And a sharp is any medical needle or other sharp object that can puncture or cut skin.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [thinking out loud] So take a new dispatcher, someone who answers calls and sends officers out. It's a busy afternoon and the phones keep ringing. Her insulin syringe sits on her desk beside her headset, and the sharps container is in the break room down the hall. Walk me through that one needle.

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: It starts with a plan for handling it and getting rid of it, BEFORE the cap comes off. She'd use a needle alternative if one's possible, and switch on any safety feature once she's done.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [skeptical] Once she's done, though, the syringe is empty. Isn't most of the risk over?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: Not at all. A little blood stays inside. And because it's so sharp, there's a high chance it accidentally pierces someone else's skin and exposes them to that blood.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: Not a comfortable thought. So now it's used and in her hand. Where does it go?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: [matter-of-fact] Straight into the sharps container. Hospitals and clinics spell out more: a used needle isn't bent, broken, recapped, removed or separated from the syringe, and it goes in immediately or as soon as possible after use.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: With the phones still going, that hallway's going to feel long. What do you say to someone who'd rather wait?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: [patient] Waiting is what the plan is for. You decide how it gets to the container before you start, use a needle alternative if there is one, switch on the safety feature if it has one, and it goes in the container the MOMENT you're done.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: This one's about a single needle and the trash can it landed in. Chris works records on nights, keeping the reports and files in order, and has a story from one of those nights. Go ahead, Chris.

lines.speaker: CHRIS
lines.text: [tired] It was near the end of my shift. I'd just taken my insulin at my desk. The sharps container was down the hall, past the copier. I knew better from training. But I had reports to finish. So I thought, just this once, and dropped the needle in the trash can under my desk.

lines.speaker: CHRIS
lines.text: At shift change, when the morning crew came in, Jacob came around to empty the cans. He grabbed my bag by the top and lifted it out. Then he stopped, pulled his hand back, and looked at it. I keep thinking about how close that container was.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [sighs] That's hard to hear. What's really at stake when a used needle goes into a trash bag?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: Whatever blood is left inside it. A needle stick can expose someone to bloodborne pathogens, meaning germs carried in blood, like H-I-V, hepatitis B and hepatitis C. Those could lead to severe health problems.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: And Jacob was only emptying a can. How does that sit with you?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: [concerned] Badly. A sharp that's thrown away wrong can hurt someone down the line who NEVER touched it.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: Chris was only trying to get reports done. What do you make of that?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: One shortcut can cause a serious injury, maybe an infection that changes a life. Where you put a needle directly affects someone else's risk.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [exhales] Just a regular bag at the end of a regular night.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [curious] Picture someone at the station about to empty the trash bins. They pull on the thickest gloves in the supply closet and figure they're covered. Do you think they are?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: Not against a needle. EVEN thick gloves can be pierced by one.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [surprised] So the thickest pair in the closet still won't stop a needle. What are the gloves good for, then?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: Plenty. Heavy-duty gloves made of nitrile, latex, vinyl or neoprene help protect hands from cuts and hazardous substances. They're P-P-E, personal protective equipment, meaning gear you wear. But P-P-E alone is less effective against needle sticks than engineering controls. Those are things like a sharps container, which deal with the needle itself instead of your hands.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: Now say an agency is deciding how to protect everyone who empties trash. It can buy cut-resistant gloves for all of them, or add sharps containers where people actually use needles. Gloves for everybody sounds quicker. Which way would you go?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: [firmly] The containers. A proper sharps container is the most effective protection, because it takes the hazard away before anyone can touch it. It closes the needle inside. That's been stated for manufacturing settings, so I'll keep it there: safety-engineered containers like that reduce needle sticks and the spread of bloodborne pathogens, the germs carried in blood.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: But a container only works if people actually walk the needle over to it. Why don't they always?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: Because it's the easy path, and people lean that way. I trained a lot of classes, and somebody was usually hunting for the shorter route. Engineering controls and training are what have to beat that habit when it comes to getting rid of sharps.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [wry] I'd have pulled on the thickest pair and gone straight for that trash bag. Now I'd trust those gloves a lot less.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: Say someone new is standing at their desk tomorrow with a used needle. Where does your mind go?

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: [thoughtful] Where the nearest sharps container is. If you were holding a used needle right now... how FAR would you have to walk to get there?

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: That walk down the hall sounds simple when nobody's busy.

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: [thoughtful] It does. What happens when someone skips it is worth hearing out.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: That container at the end of the hall is doing a lot of work.

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: More than people give it credit for. Let's stay with it a little longer.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: [exhales] That one stays with you.

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: It does. So let's look at what actually stands between a used needle and somebody's hand.

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: Next time you sit down at your desk, take a look down the hall.

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: [curious] Do you know where the nearest sharps container is from your desk, and how a used needle would get there before you ever open it?

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: Think about who empties the trash cans where you work.

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: [thoughtful] If a used needle ended up in one of those bags tonight, whose hands would find it first?

lines.speaker: DANA
lines.text: Picture yourself pulling on a pair of thick gloves before a trash run.

lines.speaker: RAY
lines.text: Then ask where the nearest sharps container is, and whether it's close enough that people actually walk a needle over to it.
